q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d %d", 7 > 3, 7 == 3);
```
x: A relational expression in C has the int value 1 when true and 0 when false, so 7 > 3 gives 1 and 7 == 3 gives 0. C prints numbers here, not the words true and false.
The ! operator gives 0 for any non-zero value and 1 for 0, so !p is 0 and !q is 1. It does not change the sign of a number, so -5 is wrong.
op holds '-', so control jumps to case '-' and prints 12 - 4 = 8; break then leaves the switch. default runs only when no case matches.
250 is not <= 100 and not <= 200, so the last branch runs: 1300 + (250 - 200) * 10 = 1300 + 500 = 1800. 2500 charges all 250 units at 10, which the ladder does not do.
p == q is false, so the first test fails. In the second test p == r (5 == 5) is true, so isosceles is printed and the else is skipped. Only one branch of an else-if ladder runs.
c holds the character '7', which lies between '0' and '9', so the second test is true and digit is printed. The first test fails because '7' is not between 'a' and 'z'.
Multiplication comes before addition, so x * 2 + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7 and case 7 prints seven. nine would need x * (2 + 1).
Control jumps to case 2 and adds 20; with no break it falls through into case 1 and adds 10, so s = 30. case 3 is above the entry point, so its 30 is never added (60 would add all three).
x > 0 is false, so the outer else block runs; inside it y > 0 is also false, so q = 3. q = 4 belongs to the branch for x > 0, which is skipped.

q: Which task is easier to program with an `if-else-if` ladder than with a `switch` statement?
o: Choosing an action for a menu choice of 1, 2 or 3
Choosing a tax rate from the range in which a `float` salary lies
Choosing an action for the operator characters `'+'`, `'-'` and `'*'`
Printing a day name for a day number from 1 to 7
x: A case label must be a single integer or character constant, so a switch cannot test ranges of a float value; an if-else-if ladder can (salary < 50000.0, and so on). The other tasks match one exact integer or character value each, which a switch does well.

q: In C, when is the condition of an `if` statement treated as false?
o: When its value is anything other than 1
When it uses a relational operator
x: C treats 0 as false and every non-zero value, negative ones included, as true. So a condition such as -3 is true, not false.
age < 12 is false because 12 is not less than 12, so the conditional operator gives 500 and fee = 1000 + 500 = 1500. 1200 comes from wrongly taking 12 < 12 as true.

q: Two `case` labels in the same `switch` statement both have the value `3`. What happens?
o: Only the first `case 3` is ever used
Both `case 3` blocks run, one after the other
x: Every case label in one switch must have a different constant value; a repeated value is a compile-time error, so the program does not run at all. C does not quietly pick the first one.

q: Which condition is equivalent to `!(p > 0 || q > 0)`?
x: By De Morgan's law, NOT (X OR Y) = (NOT X) AND (NOT Y), and NOT (p > 0) is p <= 0. Changing || to && is needed, so p <= 0 || q <= 0 is wrong; p < 0 forgets the value 0.

&& has higher precedence than ||, so the condition is x > 5 || (x < 2 && y == 0) = 1 || 0 = 1, and yes is printed. Reading it left to right as (x > 5 || x < 2) && y == 0 would wrongly give 0 and print no.

q: Which is a correct `if-else` statement in C?
x: In C the condition goes in brackets, there is no then keyword, and each simple statement ends with a semicolon. The colon form is Python-like and the then form is from other languages.
n > 0 is false, so its value is 0 and control jumps to case 0, printing not positive; break ends the switch. A relational expression is a normal int (0 or 1), so it can be the switch expression.
p > q (10 > 25) is false, so the else block runs: q = 25 - 10 = 15, then p = 10 + 15 = 25. The new value of q is used in the second statement, so 25 25 is wrong.

The inner brackets run first: r = 18 % 4 = 2, and the value of the assignment (2) is compared with 1. 2 > 1 is true, so 2 big is printed. 4 big wrongly takes the quotient 18 / 4 instead of the remainder.
Pairs: (1,10) 1 < 10 print; (3,8) print; (5,6) print; (7,4) 7 < 4 is false, so the loop stops. Both variables change in every step (i by +2, j by -2), so 2-9 never appears.
a is printed before it is updated: the values of a are 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 over the 6 passes (each new b is the sum of the old a and b). 1 1 2 3 5 8 would print b instead of a.
For i = 1 the inner loop prints 1, 2, 3; for i = 2 it prints 2, 4, 6. The inner loop finishes all its passes before i changes, so the order 1 2 2 4 3 6 is wrong.
d = 2: 27 % 2 = 1, go on. d = 3: 27 % 3 = 0, so prime = 0 and break leaves the loop with d still 3. 1 6 is what would print if no divisor were found (the loop stops when 6 * 6 > 27).
s grows 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 while i goes 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Now s < 15 is false, so the loop stops with i = 6 and s = 15. i was already increased after the last addition, so 5 15 is wrong.

q: A program must print a table of exactly 10 lines, and the number of repetitions is known before the loop starts. Which loop is normally used for this?
x: The for loop keeps the start value, the test and the update in one line, which suits a known count such as 10. do-while is chosen when the body must run at least once; switch is not a loop at all.

q: In a `while` loop, when is the condition tested?
o: After every execution of the body
Only once, before the first execution
Only when a `break` statement is reached
Before every execution of the body
x: while is an entry-controlled loop: the condition is checked before each pass, so the body may run zero times. Testing after the body is how do-while works.
i becomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. When i is 2, continue skips the addition, so s = 1 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 13. continue does not end the loop (that would be break), so 1 is wrong.
The body runs for i = 2, 5, 8, 11, so c = 4. After the pass with 11, i becomes 14, the test 14 <= 11 fails and the loop ends, so i is 14, not 11.
Odd i is added and even i is subtracted: 1 - 2 + 3 - 4 + 5 - 6 = -3. 21 adds all six numbers and 9 adds only the odd ones.
The loop counts the values of d from 1 to 12 that divide 12 exactly: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, so c = 6. 4 leaves out 1 and 12 themselves, which the test d <= n includes.
x is printed and then changed: 1 -> 3 -> 7 -> 15 -> 31. After 15 is printed x becomes 31, the test 31 < 20 fails and the loop ends, so 31 is never printed.

The outer loop runs 3 times (i = 0, 1, 2) and for each of them the inner loop runs 4 times (j = 0 to 3), so 3 x 4 = 12 stars. 7 adds the counts instead of multiplying; 20 wrongly counts 4 x 5 as if both ends were included.

q: Which `while` loop prints the same output as `for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) printf("%d ", i);`?
x: A for loop does its update after the body, so the while version must print first and then increase i, starting at 0 with the test i < 5: it prints 0 1 2 3 4. Increasing i before printing gives 1 2 3 4 5, and <= 5 adds an extra 5.
n changes 6 -> 3 -> 10 -> 5 -> 16 -> 8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1, and c counts each change: 8. The starting value 6 is not a change, so 9 counts one too many.

Remainders are printed as they are found: 13 % 2 = 1 (n -> 6), 6 % 2 = 0 (n -> 3), 3 % 2 = 1 (n -> 1), 1 % 2 = 1 (n -> 0), giving 1011. That is the binary of 13 (1101) written backwards, because the lowest bit comes out first.
i takes the values 5, 3, 1; the next value -1 fails the test i > 0, so the loop stops before printing it.

q: When a `break` statement runs inside a loop, where does control go next?
o: To the next iteration of the same loop
To the first statement after the loop
Back to the first line of `main()`
To the loop condition, which is tested again
x: break ends the loop at once and the program carries on with the statement after it. Going on to the next iteration is what continue does.
c starts at 'p' and moves 2 letters each pass: 'p', 'r', 't'. The next value 'v' is past 't', so the loop stops. pqrst would need c++ instead of c += 2.
dbl(4) = 8 is worked out first, then tri(8) = 8 + dbl(8) = 8 + 16 = 24. 12 is tri(4), which forgets that the argument was doubled first.
big returns the largest of its three arguments: big(7, 3, 11) = 11 and big(2, 9, 5) = 9, so 11 - 9 = 2.

q: A program has the prototype `float rate(int n, float p);` and a `float` variable `y`. Which statement calls `rate` correctly?
x: A call gives just the values, one for each parameter in the prototype (here two), with no type names. rate(2.5) passes too few arguments, and writing types inside a call is a syntax error.
add returns 6, but the call is not used in an assignment, so the value is simply thrown away. s itself was passed by value and is never changed, so 1 is printed.

q: A function is declared as `void show(int n);`. What happens when a program contains the statement `int k = show(4);`?
o: The compiler reports an error, because `show` returns no value
x: A void function returns nothing, so its call cannot be used as a value; the compiler rejects the statement. Passing 4 as an argument does not make 4 the returned value.
isprime returns 1 only for 2, 3, 5 and 7 (1 is rejected by n < 2, and 4, 6, 8, 9, 10 have a divisor), so c = 4. 5 wrongly counts 1 as prime.
The argument expressions are worked out before the call: a + 1 = 4 goes to x and a * 2 = 6 goes to y, so x - y = 4 - 6 = -2. Taking them in the other order gives 2.

o: The compiler reports an error, because `k` is not visible at the `printf`
x: k is a local variable of the inner block { }, so it exists only inside that block; using it in the printf after the block is a compile error. Inside the block t was changed to 7, but the program never runs.

Inside main the local t (10) hides the global t. inc() changes only the global t (4 -> 5 -> 6); main prints its own local t, which is still 10. 6 is the global value, which main cannot see by that name.

q: In the function definition `int max(int a, int b) { ... }`, the first line `int max(int a, int b)` is called the:
x: The header (declarator) gives the return type, the name and the parameters, and the body in braces follows it. A prototype looks similar but stands alone and ends with a semicolon.

q: The built-in functions `sqrt()` and `pow()` are declared in which header file?
x: The mathematical library functions such as sqrt, pow and fabs are declared in math.h. stdio.h declares input/output functions such as printf and scanf.
pow(2, 5) is 2 to the power 5 = 32, and sqrt(49) is the square root, 7; %.0f prints them with no decimals. 10 is 2 x 5 and 25 is 5 squared, both misreadings of pow.

q: In the call `area(5, 3)`, the values 5 and 3 are called the:
x: Values written in a call are the actual arguments; they are copied into the formal parameters named in the function's header. The return value is what comes back, not what is sent.

first returns the smallest divisor from 2 upwards: 35 % 5 == 0 is the first hit (35 is odd and 35 % 3 = 2, 35 % 4 = 3), so 5. 13 has no divisor below 13, so the loop ends and return n gives 13. 7 is a divisor of 35 but is found after 5.

q: What does the word `void` mean in the prototype `int getnum(void);`?
o: The function can return a value of any type
The function can take any number of arguments
x: void inside the brackets says the parameter list is empty, so getnum is called as getnum(). The return type here is int; a function that returns nothing has void before its name instead.
The inner call show(3) runs first: it prints 3 and returns 6. The outer call show(6) prints 6 and returns 12, which goes into r and is printed last.
Inside the function x * 2 = 5.4, but the return type is int, so the value is converted to int by dropping the fraction: 5. It is not rounded to 6, and %d could not print 5.4.

q: Which is a main advantage of dividing a C program into functions?
o: The program no longer needs a `main()` function
The same code can be called many times instead of being written again
Variables no longer need to be declared
The program is always free of errors
x: A function is written once and called wherever it is needed, which saves repeated code and makes the program easier to test and change. Every C program still needs main(), and functions do not remove errors by themselves.

q: What does `fclose(fp)` do?
o: Deletes the file from the disk
Erases all the data stored in the file
Writes any data still in the buffer to the file and releases the file
Moves to the start of the file so it can be read again
x: fclose finishes work on a file: data waiting in the buffer is written out and the file is released. The file and its contents stay on the disk.
fputs writes the string exactly as given and adds no space or newline, so the two strings sit side by side: GoodDay. The file is opened once with "w", so the second fputs does not wipe the first.

fgets(s, 4, fp) reads at most 4 - 1 = 3 characters (one place is kept for the '\0' at the end of the string), so s holds Lah. It would stop earlier only at a newline, and it never reads past one into Karachi.
Only the newline characters are counted, and each of the three lines ends with one, so n = 3. 11 counts the letters and 14 counts every character, letters and newlines together.

o: Adds the contents of `old.txt` to the end of what `new.txt` already holds
Moves the text out of `old.txt`, leaving it empty
Prints the contents of `old.txt` on the screen
x: Each character read from old.txt with fgetc is written to new.txt with fputc until EOF, so new.txt becomes a copy. new.txt is opened with "w", which starts it empty, so nothing is added to old contents; old.txt is only read, so it is unchanged.

q: A text file stores its data as:
o: the exact memory bytes of variables, which do not read as text
machine code that the CPU runs directly
characters that can be read in a text editor such as Notepad
x: A text file holds a sequence of characters (letters, digits, spaces, newlines), so it can be opened and read in any text editor. Storing the raw memory bytes of variables is what a binary file does.

"w" creates n.txt with 4 7, and "a" adds 10 at the end instead of wiping it, so the file holds 4 7 10. fscanf reads the three numbers and stops at the end, giving s = 4 + 7 + 10 = 21. 10 would be right only if "a" erased the file like "w".
%s reads the word Sara (it stops at the space) and %d reads the number 85 into m. m + 5 is added as numbers, giving 90, not joined as text (855).

q: What does the statement `fprintf(stdout, "%d", 5 * 4);` do?
o: Writes 20 into a disk file named `stdout`
Causes an error, because `fprintf` works only with disk files
x: stdout is the standard output stream (the screen), opened automatically, so fprintf(stdout, ...) works like printf and shows 20. The expression 5 * 4 is worked out before printing.

q: Which pair of functions reads and writes formatted data, such as numbers with `%d`, in a text file?
x: fscanf and fprintf work like scanf and printf but take a FILE pointer, so they read and write formatted values in a file. fgetc and fputc handle one character at a time, and scanf/printf use the keyboard and screen.
